e.meaning: flower (Arabic zahra), or a form of Sarah, princess
e.etymology: A 20th-century name explained either as a variant of Sarah or from Arabic zahra, flower. Princess Anne chose it for her daughter in 1981, which brought it to wide notice.
namesakes: Zara Tindall (British royal and Olympic equestrian)

assoc.t: Spanish fast-fashion clothing chain

e.etymology: From an English surname, from Middle English palmer, a pilgrim who had been to the Holy Land and brought back a palm branch as proof.

assoc.t: Arnold Palmer, golfer and the iced tea and lemonade drink
Palmer's cocoa butter lotion

e.etymology: A modern American spelling of Brinley, an English surname and place name meaning burned clearing. It can also be read as a blend of Bryn and Lee.
From Greek Alexis, helper or defender, from the same verb as Alexander. A man's name in Greek and French, it has gone mostly to girls in the US since actress Alexis Smith in the 1940s.

e.meaning: form of Leah, a Hebrew name read as weary or wild cow
e.etymology: The Latin, Italian and Spanish form of the Biblical Leah, wife of Jacob. It also arises as a short form of names ending in -lia, such as Julia, Amelia and Rosalia.
Borrowed in the 19th century from the Russian virtue name Vera, faith. It has also long been linked with Latin vera, true.

assoc.t: aloe vera, the plant and skin gel
Vera Wang, bridal and fashion designer label
Vera Bradley quilted handbags and luggage

e.etymology: The spelling of Stephen that matches how it is said, from Greek stephanos, a crown or wreath. Saint Stephen in the Book of Acts is regarded as the first Christian martyr.
From Greek daphne, the laurel or bay tree. In Greek myth Daphne is a nymph who is turned into a laurel to escape the god Apollo.

assoc.t: Daphne Blake of Scooby-Doo
Daphne Bridgerton of Netflix's Bridgerton
nymph of Greek myth turned into a laurel tree

e.etymology: The Spanish, Portuguese and South Slavic form of Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, grace. It honors Saint Anne, by tradition the mother of the Virgin Mary.
The medieval English form of Jeremiah, the Hebrew prophet whose name means the Lord exalts. It has also been used in Ireland to anglicize Diarmaid.
namesakes: Jeremy Allen White (star of The Bear)

assoc.t: 1991 Pearl Jam song about a troubled schoolboy

e.meaning: weir, from the English town of Crewe
e.etymology: From the surname Crew or Crewe, after Crewe in Cheshire, whose name comes from Old Welsh criu, a weir. Today it is also heard as the English word crew, a team.

assoc.t: J.Crew clothing retailer
crew, the sport of rowing

e.etymology: The French feminine form of Vivian, from the Latin saints' names Vivianus and Viviana, probably from vivus, alive.
From the English word king, Old English cyning. It is also a surname that began as a nickname for someone who carried himself like a king or served in a royal household.
namesakes: Martin Luther King Jr. (civil rights leader)

assoc.t: a male monarch; also the chess piece and playing card
Martin Luther King Jr., civil rights leader (surname)

e.etymology: From Arabic zayn, beauty or adornment. Singer Zayn Malik of One Direction made this spelling familiar to English speakers.

assoc.t: Zayn Malik, pop singer formerly of One Direction

e.etymology: From Arabic Umar, from a root meaning to live long or thrive; Umar was the second caliph of Islam. A separate Hebrew Omar appears in Genesis as a grandson of Esau.
A pet form of Steven, Stephen and Stephanie, all from Greek stephanos, crown. Long a nickname, it is now given in its own right, mostly to girls.

assoc.t: Stevie Nicks and Stevie Wonder, music legends

e.etymology: From the Roman family name Paulus, from Latin paulus, small. Saul of Tarsus took it as the apostle Paul, whose letters make up much of the New Testament.
namesakes: Paul the Apostle (New Testament missionary and letter writer)

e.etymology: A respelling of Cash, an English occupational surname and a variant of Case, a maker of boxes and chests. It is also a short form of Indian names such as Kashyap.
namesakes: Kash Patel (FBI director under President Trump)

assoc.t: sounds like cash, money

e.etymology: From the Swahili word zuri, good or beautiful. It came into use among African American families and has been a top 1,000 US girls' name since 2010.
In American use mostly a spelling of Aaliyah, from Arabic aliya, exalted. It is also the Hebrew word aliyah, ascent, used for going up to read the Torah and for moving to Israel.

assoc.t: Aaliyah, the late R&B singer, spelled with two a's
aliyah, Jewish immigration to Israel

e.etymology: From Irish Rónán, from rón, seal, with a diminutive ending. Several early Irish saints bore the name, and it is also traditional in Brittany.

assoc.t: Ronan the Accuser, Guardians of the Galaxy villain

e.meaning: settlement of a man named Paecc
e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English for the settlement of a man called Paecc. The nickname Pax happens to be the Latin word for peace.
namesakes: Bill Paxton (actor in Twister and Aliens)

e.etymology: A respelling of the Hawaiian name Kailani, from kai, sea, and lani, sky or heaven, shaped by the familiar look of Kayla.
From Hebrew Noa, movement, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad in the Book of Numbers; it is unrelated to Noah. For boys it is also the Hawaiian form of Noah.
e.note: Sounds the same as the boys' name Noah, so expect spelling mix-ups.

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English for rock hill or army hill. As a girls' name it recalls the 1930s film star Jean Harlow.

assoc.t: Jean Harlow, 1930s Hollywood blonde bombshell

e.etymology: From French Rémy, a short form of the Latin name Remigius, traditionally derived from remex, oarsman. Saint Remigius baptized Clovis, king of the Franks.

assoc.t: the rat chef in Pixar's Ratatouille
Rémy Martin cognac

e.etymology: From the English word and musical term harmony, from Greek harmonia. Harmonia was the Greek goddess of concord.
The name of the Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, from an old Italic root meaning divine or shining. English speakers took it up in the 16th century.
namesakes: Diana Ross (lead singer of the Supremes)

assoc.t: Diana, Princess of Wales
Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon
Diana Prince, Wonder Woman's real name

e.meaning: of the Julius family; traditionally read as youthful
e.etymology: The feminine form of the Latin name Julianus, a derivative of Julius, the Roman family name of Julius Caesar. Several early saints were named Juliana.

e.meaning: woodland clearing by a boundary, or pleasant clearing
e.etymology: From an English surname taken from several places called Marley, Old English for a boundary, pleasant or marten woodland clearing. Reggae star Bob Marley made it familiar worldwide.

assoc.t: Bob Marley, reggae legend
the unruly Labrador of Marley & Me
Jacob Marley, the ghost in A Christmas Carol

e.etymology: Either from Selene, the Greek goddess of the moon, or a variant of Selina, from Latin Caelina, heavenly. US use surged in 1995, the year the Tejano singer Selena died.

assoc.t: Selena, the Queen of Tejano music

e.etymology: A modern name of uncertain origin, probably a feminine form of Nyle or Niles, helped along by similar names such as Kyla and Nia.
